status: Proposed study design only; no participants recruited or results collected
question: Does native-language experience help readers identify and model an agglutinative inscription after controlling for training in the script?
profiles: Record all fluent languages, native and learned; knowledge of Kazakh and other agglutinative morphology; actual cuneiform experience; prior exposure to each inscription. Avoid treating national identity as language competence.
matching: Compare readers with similar training in sign identification and equal access to source images. Keep previous exposure to translations as a separate variable.
procedure: preselect high-resolution photos and an unreadable negative control before content analysis
collect image-only annotations with neutral sign IDs
freeze proposed boundaries and recurrence predictions
evaluate those predictions on held-out views or witnesses
then collect explicit competing sound and meaning hypotheses
check each hypothesis against separately held-out ancient phonetic/bilingual evidence, retaining ambiguity
outcomes: agreement on visible marks and reproducible boundaries, without calling agreement truth
successful versus failed predictions on held-out material
changes made after access to other editions
number of ad hoc rule changes needed for each language hypothesis
prohibited_shortcuts: do not score conventional translations as unquestioned ground truth
do not score Kazakh resemblance as unquestioned ground truth
do not count reading the same edition twice as independent confirmation
do not claim reader-group effects without actual comparable participant data
limits: No available experiment in this project establishes a native-language effect yet; image structure alone does not uniquely determine pronunciation or meaning
